name: edbrowse
why: A text-mode browser built around the ed editor, a genuinely odd way to browse the web.

brief.what_it_is: Edbrowse is a combination editor, browser, and mail client that is 100% text based, with an interface similar to /bin/ed. It can edit several files at once and render HTML, and it can be driven from scripts: a batch job or cron job can fetch pages, submit forms, and send email without a human present. It can also query databases over ODBC. The executables listed are edbrowse plus plugins for chrome, mpv, telnet, and zip.
brief.why_it_exists: It was written for blind users, and the inspiration came from author Karl Dahlke's years as a blind computer user; the site describes it as a command-line philosophy piece in its own right. Many sighted users now use it for its scripting capabilities, which the site says can be found nowhere else.
brief.how_it_works: You drive it with ed-style line commands rather than a mouse or full-screen menus, and it renders HTML into text you can edit. The homepage says the JavaScript engine has changed over time: a home-grown engine, then SpiderMonkey in 3.1.1, then duktape, then quickjs, and now quickjs-ng. The README does not explain the rendering pipeline further.

commands_seen.context: From the README: converts the user's guide to plain text with lynx so you can read it in an editor, since the guide is best read in a browser and edbrowse is not yet installed.
From the homepage: clones the GitHub wiki, which has tips, tricks, and sample .ebrc configurations. The site notes the last slash in the wiki URL becomes a dot in the clone URL.

brief.install_notes: Intended for Unix-like systems. To compile you need the pcre-devel and libcurl-devel packages (on Linux these may come from the development install set). Version 3.8.15 and later require the quickjs-ng JavaScript engine. The homepage offers statically linked Linux binaries (version 3.8.17 is mentioned) for people who do not want to build from source. The README links to doc/installing.md for build steps, which I did not fetch, so I cannot confirm the full build procedure or any configuration needed on first run. The user's guide recommends reading it before first use, because the interface has few built-in help facilities.
brief.standout: The README calls it the only fully command-based browser of its kind as far as the authors know. Its design goal is unusual: it treats batch automation of the web (cron jobs that submit forms and send mail) as a first-class use, alongside ed-style editing of text and HTML.
brief.status: Appears maintained. The homepage cites a recent stable release (3.8.17 static binaries), a requirement for quickjs-ng from 3.8.15 onward, and an active mailing list and IRC channel. I did not find a release date or last-commit date in the pages I read, so the exact recency is unverified.
brief.caveats: The README includes a disclaimer that the software is provided as-is and might trash your files or send bad data across the Internet. It is described as dense, with many cryptic one- and two-letter commands and few interactive help facilities, so the user's guide is effectively required reading. It is intended for Unix-like platforms, and the perl version 1.5.17 is unsupported and undocumented, lacking JavaScript support. The project calls itself a work in progress and says it is short on developers. The license is in a LICENSE file, which I did not read, so I cannot state its terms. The homepage was reachable.
quotes: This is a fully command based browser, the only one of its kind as far as we know.
A batch job, or cron job, can access web pages on the internet, submit forms, and send email, with no human intervention whatsoever.
It contains many cryptic one and two letter commands, and few interactive help facilities.
fetch_log: https://edbrowse.org: fetched OK, returned the homepage text (not a GitHub repo, so the README was not returned).
https://github.com/edbrowse/edbrowse: fetched OK, returned the README.

judge.reason: An ed-style text browser that can automate web pages, submit forms, and send email from scripts is a genuinely unusual way to interact with the web.

entry.title: edbrowse
entry.tldr: A web browser, editor and mail client driven by ed-style line commands, built by a blind programmer and scriptable enough to run web tasks from cron.
entry.deeper_look:
Edbrowse is a text-only editor, browser and mail client with an interface modelled on /bin/ed. You type short line commands instead of using a mouse or full-screen menus. It renders HTML into text you can edit, can work on several files at once, and can query databases over ODBC. It also runs JavaScript. The engine has been swapped several times over the years: a home-grown one, then SpiderMonkey, duktape, quickjs, and now quickjs-ng.

It was written for blind users, drawing on author Karl Dahlke's years as a blind computer user. A line-oriented interface reads cleanly through a screen reader or speech synthesiser, and nothing depends on where things sit on screen. The site calls it a command-line philosophy piece in its own right.

The idea underneath is that the web can be a stream of text you edit and script, not a picture you look at. Many sighted users now use it for that reason. In the project's words: "A batch job, or cron job, can access web pages on the internet, submit forms, and send email, with no human intervention whatsoever." The README says it is "a fully command based browser, the only one of its kind as far as we know."

The commands are terse, one or two letters, and there is little built-in help. The user's guide is the way in, and it is worth reading before the first session.
entry.install:
brew install edbrowse
# Intended for Unix-like systems. Building from source needs pcre and libcurl development packages, and version 3.8.15 or later needs quickjs-ng.

From the README: converts the user's guide to plain text so you can read it in an editor before edbrowse is installed.
Clones the project wiki, which holds tips, tricks and sample .ebrc configuration files.

entry.whats_unique: It treats unattended web automation, such as cron jobs that submit forms and send mail, as a first-class use alongside ed-style editing. The project says that scripting is found nowhere else.
entry.caveats: The README warns it is provided as-is and might trash your files or send bad data across the Internet, and the cryptic commands make the user's guide effectively required reading.
